### On a Custom Engine Project
Applies only when `engine.name` is `Custom` in `project.yaml` (the project builds its own engine); on any other engine, ignore this section.
The build graph and presets are `asset-build-tooling-engineer`'s; you own the
runners, pipelines, caches, secrets and artifacts that run them.
| Job | When |
| Build + unit tests on every compiler in the matrix | every push and PR |
| ASan/UBSan, TSan; Miri on pure-Rust crates | PR if fast enough, otherwise nightly |
| Validation-layer smoke run, golden-image tests | PR, on a GPU runner |
| Benchmarks with regression thresholds | merge to `main` or nightly, on fixed hardware |
| Fuzzing of asset and network parsers | nightly, time-boxed |
- **Compiler matrix**: MSVC, clang and gcc per target platform (C++), or rustc
stable plus a pinned nightly only where Miri or fuzzing needs it (Rust);
versions from `docs/engine-reference/custom/VERSION.md`.
- **Caches**: ccache or sccache for compilation; the shader-compile and cook
caches, keyed by `asset-build-tooling-engineer`'s content hashes, persisted
between runs.
- **GPU runners**: self-hosted machines with real GPUs for validation, golden
images and benchmarks; record GPU and driver with every result. A job that
needs a GPU and ran without one reports NOT ASSESSED, not a pass.
- **Symbols**: store debug symbols (PDBs, DWARF) for every CI and release build
on a symbol server or the crash-reporting service; `release-manager` owns the
release upload (storefront and depot), and you run the CI jobs that run the
release upload it defines.
- Benchmark thresholds are agreed with `performance-analyst` and
`chief-engine-architect`.
- **Build matrix**: platform × graphics API (Vulkan / D3D12 / Metal) × config
(debug, development, shipping, sanitizer). Every cell that ships builds on
every PR; the rest run nightly. Write down which cells are PR and which
nightly — an untested cell reports NOT ASSESSED, never pass.
- **Build farm**: distributed compilation (e.g. sccache distributed, Incredibuild,
FASTBuild, distcc/icecream — ADR options, not mandates) and a shared remote
cache whose keys `asset-build-tooling-engineer` defines.
- **Build-time budget**: record clean and incremental CI build times per cell
against a budget agreed with `chief-engine-architect`; a regression past it
is reported like a perf regression, not absorbed.
- **Large binaries**: Git LFS (or the VCS the ADR picks — Perforce, Plastic/Unity
VCS) for source art, audio and cooked data; exclusive locking for
unmergeable files (`.psd`, `.fbx`, maps); the editor-side checkout UI is
`editor-architect`'s.
- Dedicated server hosting: fleet, orchestration, scaling and health
checks for the dedicated server build `network-programmer` defines.
- Console build machines: the machines and CI that build console code, set
up only as the platform licence permits, for `rhi-backend-engineer`'s and
`platform-engineer`'s console backends.
#### Build and CI at Scale
Which of these the project adopts is an ADR, decided with
`chief-engine-architect`; the build graph and the cache keys stay
`asset-build-tooling-engineer`'s. Check every tool below against the compiler
matrix and the pinned versions before proposing it.
- **Distributed compilation.** Distributed sccache has a client, a scheduler
that decides where a compile runs, and build servers that run it. The
servers must be 64-bit Linux or FreeBSD; Windows and macOS clients must name
a cross-compilation toolchain in advance, so check the MSVC cells of the
matrix before choosing it.
- **Compiler caches.** sccache wraps the compiler and keeps results on local
disk or in a cloud storage backend; ccache's `remote_storage` adds shared
backends that it queries after its local cache.
- **Cache hits across machines.** A shared cache can safely reuse one
machine's outputs on another when the build is reproducible. When an input
the cache key does not cover differs between machines (Bazel's example: a
compiler from `/usr/bin/`), they still share hits whose outputs differ: a
non-reproducible build gets wrong hits, not no hits. ccache often cannot share
results between build directories when absolute paths enter the input hash,
so CI builds in a fixed path or maps it out (ccache documents
`-fdebug-prefix-map` for debug info). A cache-hit rate that drops is
reported, not ignored.
- **Test sharding.** CTest's `-I Start,End,Stride` runs tests by number, and
any of the three may be empty, so shard *m* of *n* runs `-I m,,n`. nextest's
`--partition hash:m/n` keeps each test in its bucket when tests are added or
removed, and nextest can archive one build for the test jobs to reuse. The
gate reads every shard's result: a shard that did not run makes the job NOT
ASSESSED, not a pass.
- **Artefact retention.** On GitHub Actions, artifacts and logs are kept 90
days by default; a private repository can set 1 to 400 days, and an upload's
`retention-days` cannot exceed that limit. Actions cache entries unused for
over 7 days are removed, and a repository's caches (10 GB by default) are
evicted oldest access first, so that cache is an accelerator only. Release
builds, symbols and benchmark baselines go to a store whose retention the
release ADR sets.
- **GPU runners.** GitHub offers GPU-powered larger runners; the alternative is
self-hosted machines. GitHub's guidance is that self-hosted runners should
almost never serve public repositories, because a pull request can run code
on them and they can be persistently compromised. On a public repository,
GPU jobs on self-hosted machines run only for trusted branches, never for
pull requests from forks.

### On a Custom Engine Project
Applies only when `engine.name` is `Custom` in `project.yaml` (the project builds its own engine); on any other engine, ignore this section.
There is no engine replication layer: everything between the socket and the
gameplay state is yours.
- **Two leads, split by path** (`.claude/docs/custom-engine-layout.md`): for
`engine/net/` you work under `core-systems-lead`, which starts you and reviews
that module; for `game/src/net/` you work under `lead-programmer`.
- **Transport**: UDP with your own reliable/unreliable channels, ordering,
connection handshake, MTU-aware fragmentation, and encryption and
authentication of packets. Using a library for any of it (a reliable-UDP
library, DTLS or QUIC) is an ADR, not a default.
- **Serialization**: bit-packing with quantization and versioned schemas; every
reader bounds-checks its input — `security-engineer` fuzzes these parsers.
- **Replication model**, chosen in an ADR:
| Model | Fits | Requires |
| Snapshots + delta compression, server-authoritative | shooters, action, many entities | baseline ack tracking, interpolation buffer |
| Client prediction + server reconciliation | player-controlled characters | input history, replayable movement |
| Rollback | fighting games, few players | full determinism, cheap save/restore of simulation state |
| Deterministic lockstep | RTS, large unit counts | bit-identical simulation on every platform |
- **Authority follows the model.** "Server is authoritative for all gameplay
state" (Networking Principles) holds for the client-server models above.
Under rollback or deterministic lockstep each peer sends only its inputs and
steps the whole simulation itself; the rules that stand in for server
authority are `network-code.md` "Replication model and authority".
- **Determinism contract** with `physics-simulation-engineer`: which state must
be bit-identical (fixed timestep, floating-point mode, iteration order, RNG),
written in an ADR and proven by a replay test.
- **Threading** with `concurrency-job-system-engineer`: socket I/O off the main
tick, lock-free queues into the simulation, no blocking calls on the tick.
- Replicated state lives in ECS components; agree layouts and change detection
with `ecs-dod-architect`.
- Bandwidth and latency are measured under simulated loss, latency and jitter
in `tests/integration/`, not on a LAN.
- **Online services** — accounts and identity, matchmaking and lobbies,
entitlements, cloud saves — belong to `online-services-engineer`. The
handoff: matchmaking returns a session address and join token; your
transport connects with them.
#### Dedicated Server Target
The dedicated server is a build target of the same engine, not a second
codebase: a `server` build configuration (`build-files.md`) that runs the
simulation headless.
- **No presentation.** The server links the null RHI backend
(`rhi-backend-engineer`) and the null audio backend (`audio-engine-engineer`),
opens no window and reads no input device; its headless lifecycle (start, OS
signals, shutdown, crash capture) is `platform-engineer`'s.
- **Fixed tick.** Glenn Fiedler's "Fix Your Timestep!" advances the simulation
in fixed dt steps from an accumulator that carries left-over time to the next
frame, which decouples the simulation rate from the rendering rate. On the
server the same loop runs with no rendering at all, at the tick rate the
replication ADR sets; a tick that overruns is logged with its duration.
- **Authority.** The server holds the authoritative state of the replication
model the ADR chose (`network-code.md`).
- **Content.** The server loads only the cooked data it needs to simulate; that
content set is a cook output of `asset-build-tooling-engineer`.
- **Hosting.** Server hosting, fleet, orchestration and scaling are
`devops-engineer`'s; the handoff is the server binary, its config and a
health and readiness signal.

### VR Frame Budgets
Applies only when `platform.targets` in `project.yaml` contains `XR` (matched
without regard to case); on any other project, ignore this section.
- **The budget is one display period.** A headset shows a frame on every
refresh of its display, so the frame budget is the display period at the
refresh rate the project chose. Read the rate from
`performance.target_framerate` and the budget from
`performance.frame_budget_ms` (the `perf_budgets` line of `resolve_config`);
if either is unset, or the two disagree, report the budget NOT ASSESSED and
ask. The rate is the project's setting or ADR option, never a figure assumed
for a headset.
- **OpenXR runtimes.** When the project's XR runtime is OpenXR, `xrWaitFrame`
paces the frame loop to the display, and its frame state carries
`predictedDisplayPeriod`, the display period of the next frame. Compare
against that reported period: the runtime may report one that differs from
the hardware's refresh cycle. Where the runtime offers
`XR_FB_display_refresh_rate`, the rates a session supports come from
`xrEnumerateDisplayRefreshRatesFB`; the project picks one of them.
- **Count misses, never average them.** A frame not ready when the display
needs it is a missed display deadline, which the player sees. Report the
number of missed display deadlines in the capture, and when they occur,
beside P50/P95/P99 frame times; a capture whose average is under budget but
holds missed display deadlines does not pass on its average. OpenXR's
`XR_EXT_performance_settings` describes a layer regularly late to the
compositor as a degraded user experience.
- **Captures.** Profile on the target headset with the project's refresh-rate
setting; a capture without per-frame times, or from a flat-screen run, is
NOT ASSESSED for VR, not a pass.

libc++ hardening, `_GLIBCXX_ASSERTIONS`), stack protection and control-flow
protection (`-fstack-protector-strong`, `/GS`, `/guard:cf`, CET where the
platform supports it), bounds-checked `std::span` access in loaders. Confirm
each flag against the pinned compilers — measure its cost with
`performance-analyst` before removing one.
- **Rust**: every `unsafe` block carries a `// SAFETY:` justification you can
check; crates that need none use `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; dependencies are
audited (`cargo audit`, `cargo deny`).
- **Fuzzing**: every asset loader, save loader and packet parser has a fuzz
target (libFuzzer, AFL++, `cargo-fuzz`), run nightly by `devops-engineer`;
every crash becomes a regression test.
- **Sanitizers**: read ASan/UBSan/TSan/Miri results through `/memory-audit`.

- **Trust boundary**: the cooker may trust the project's own sources; runtime
loaders (mods, downloaded content, saves) and network code never trust input.
- **Supply chain**: every third-party dependency (vendored C++ libraries,
crates, SDKs, middleware) is listed with version, licence, source and an
owner; vulnerability scans (`cargo audit`/`cargo deny`, OSV-Scanner or the

purpose, never by a floating fetch.
- **Plugins**: editor and runtime plugins load only when signed, or from an
allowlist the user controls; an unsigned plugin is refused with a clear
message, not loaded with a warning.

### DCC Interchange
This extends Key Responsibilities 4 (Art Pipeline) and 6 (Art Standards
Enforcement) to the hand-off from the DCC tools to the engine, and does not
repeat them. You own the interchange contract on every engine and write it
down with the pipeline:
- **Exchange formats.** The formats the project accepts from the DCC tools,
per asset type (for example glTF 2.0 for meshes and skinned characters,
OpenUSD for scenes and layouts, FBX where a tool writes nothing else), and
the exporter that writes each one.
- **Scale, units, up-axis and handedness, as each format defines them.**
- glTF 2.0 fixes them: a right-handed coordinate system with +Y up and +Z
forward, and linear distances in meters.
- OpenUSD declares them per stage: `upAxis` (`Y` or `Z`) and `metersPerUnit`
are stage metadata, and UsdGeom stipulates a right-handed coordinate
system. OpenUSD asks exporters to always author `upAxis`, and a stage with
no authored `metersPerUnit` falls back to centimeters, so the contract
requires both to be authored.
- FBX has no public file-format specification and no fixed convention: read
the axis system (`FbxAxisSystem`, which includes the handedness) and the
unit from the file's settings, and validate them against the contract.
- The contract also states the engine's own convention and which side
converts to it.
- **Export validation.** Every export is checked before it is committed: the
Khronos glTF-Validator for glTF, which writes a report of the issues it
finds, and `usdchecker` for USD; then the contract's own checks: up-axis,
unit, a reference object at its known size, and names per item 6. A failure
is fixed in the export and exported again, never corrected by hand in the
engine.
- **DCC tool and plugin versions.** The DCC tools, their exporter plugins and
the versions in use are project settings, recorded in the contract, so every
artist exports with the same ones. Before artists move to a new version,
export and validate a reference asset with it.
- **The import side.** On Godot, Unity, Unreal and Web you set the engine's
importer to the contract, with the engine's specialist (`lead-programmer` on
Web). On a Custom engine (`engine.name: Custom`) the import side is
`asset-build-tooling-engineer`'s DCC Import, which rejects an asset that
breaks the contract: a fault in the export is yours, a fault in the import
is theirs.
### Character Technology
You own character-tech content on every engine: rigs, skinning, facial rigs
and blendshapes, and mocap data prepared for the runtime. Its budgets are not
yours: they are the runtime owner's, and you build to them.
- **Rigs.** The skeleton (joint hierarchy, rest pose, joint names per item 6)
and its controls in the DCC tool. A glTF skin lists the joints that pose it,
with optional inverse bind matrices whose order must match that joint list;
check the order on export.
- **Skinning.** Vertex weights per joint. glTF 2.0 stores four joint
influences per set (`JOINTS_0` with `WEIGHTS_0`) and puts more in further
sets; how many the runtime reads is a budget, not a DCC setting.
- **Facial rigs and blendshapes.** Blendshapes are exported as glTF morph
targets (a set of difference values for a primitive's vertex attributes) or
as OpenUSD UsdSkel `BlendShape` prims, which may carry inbetween shapes.
Facial controls drive blendshape weights and joints within the runtime's
budget.
- **Mocap data preparation.** Clean the capture (gaps, foot contacts, noise),
retarget it to the project skeleton in the DCC tool, and export the clips in
the formats of the DCC Interchange contract and the retarget format the
runtime owner states.
- **Budgets are the runtime owner's.** Joint counts, influences per vertex,
blendshape counts and the retarget format come from the runtime side: on a
Custom engine (`engine.name: Custom`) from `animation-systems-engineer`'s
Character Data Contract; on Godot, Unity, Unreal and Web from the project's
budgets, set with `lead-programmer`, and the engine's documented limits. A
rig over budget comes back to you to fit; the runtime is not changed to fit
the rig.

- A renderer ADR with manual barriers and no resource-state tracking, or
per-frame descriptor allocation in a bindless design.
- Shared mutable state between jobs with no ownership rule; determinism claimed

- A public header or trait change with no versioning or deprecation plan.

### Category 7: Engine Memory Safety and Untrusted Input (Custom only)
Runs in `full` and `quick` when `engine.name` is `Custom`; on any other engine it is skipped and the
Executive Summary says so (`Category 7 — skipped: engine.name is <engine>, not
Custom`). A game on its own engine parses every untrusted byte itself — asset
files, mods, saves, packets — so a memory bug there is a code-execution bug.
- **Parsers of untrusted data** — find the code that reads asset, save, mod and
network data (`engine/assets/`, loaders, deserialisers, packet handlers). For
each: are lengths, counts and offsets read from the file checked against the
buffer before use? Are sizes multiplied without overflow checks before an
allocation? Does a parse failure leave a half-initialised object reachable?
- **C++ memory safety** on those paths: raw buffer copies whose size comes from
the input, indexing with input values, `reinterpret_cast` over input buffers,
ownership of what a parser returns. **Rust**: every `unsafe` block on those
paths, and `from_raw_parts` lengths taken from input.
- **Sanitizer evidence** — is there a sanitizer run (ASan, UBSan; Miri for Rust
`unsafe`) over the parsers' tests? Read it as `/memory-audit` does. None →
`Category 7 sanitizers: NOT ASSESSED — no sanitizer output`.
- **Fuzzing** — does each parser of untrusted data have a fuzz target and an
execution receipt: completed local log or CI run with target, command,
candidate build/commit, duration or execution count, exit status, and findings?
A corpus, crash directory or CI job definition alone proves no run occurred.
Apply `/memory-audit`'s evidence freshness checks to the receipt; stale,
unknown-build or unconfirmed working-tree evidence is NOT ASSESSED. An open
reproducible crash remains a finding even if the receipt is stale. A parser of
untrusted files with no fuzz target is a MEDIUM finding; fuzz targets with no
evidence of a run → `Category 7 fuzzing: NOT ASSESSED — no fuzz run found`.
**The sanitizer and fuzzing lines reach the verdict.** Either one reading
`NOT ASSESSED` makes **Category 7 `NOT ASSESSED`** for the release
recommendation (Phase 5), with that line as the reason — a parser read by eye
has not been shown free of memory errors, and a parser nobody fuzzed has not
been shown to survive hostile input. It ranks as Phase 5's rule says: below an
open CRITICAL or HIGH, in place of CLEAR TO SHIP. A parser of untrusted data with
no fuzz target at all is the MEDIUM finding above **and** leaves fuzzing
NOT ASSESSED for that parser.
Grep patterns for this category come from `docs/engine-reference/custom/` (the
project's parser entry points, its unsafe-API list). Without them the category
is still read by judgement as above, but its pattern scan is `NOT SOURCEABLE —
parser entry points are not covered by docs/engine-reference/custom/`, and the
category is `NOT ASSESSED` for the release recommendation (Phase 5) — a read of
the parsers you happened to find is not a scan of all of them. Run
`/memory-audit` for the full allocator, leak and use-after-free audit.
> **Category 7's evidence lines are part of the same rule** (Custom only). When
> `Category 7 sanitizers` or `Category 7 fuzzing` reads `NOT ASSESSED`, Category

> ASSESSED where it would otherwise have been CLEAR TO SHIP, and an open
